sources.record: Antonio de Morga, *Sucesos de las islas Filipinas* (Mexico, 1609), trans. Henry E. J. Stanley, *The Philippine Islands, Moluccas, Siam, Cambodia, Japan, and China, at the Close of the Sixteenth Century* (Hakluyt Society, London, 1868), pp. 336, 340, 347.
sources.perspective: A judge (*oidor*) of the Manila Audiencia, writing for a European readership about 35 years after 1573. Context for the 1570s, not a witness.

position.role: Spanish judge of the Manila Audiencia

sources.record: *Ming Shi-lu*, Wanli year 17, month 4, day 20 (2 June 1589), trans. Geoff Wade, *Southeast Asia in the Ming Shi-lu: an open access resource* (Singapore: Asia Research Institute and NUS Press).
sources.form: Primary document, court record, English translation by a named translator
sources.perspective: The Ming court's historians. The standpoint is imperial: security, licensing, tax. Merchants are subjects, not authors.

sources.record: Alonso Fernández de Castro, *Principal points in regard to the trade of the Filipinas*, [1602?]. B&R vol. 12 (Cleveland, 1904), pp. 46 ff. (used pp. 50–51). Translated from the Spanish by Jose M. and Clara M. Asensio and Emma Helen Blair.
sources.perspective: A lawyer arguing for restrictions on Mexican and Peruvian trade. The date is B&R's guess.

position.audience: The crown, via a printed pamphlet
position.interests: Restricting the Mexican and Peruvian trade

sources.record: Dennis O. Flynn and Arturo Giráldez, "Born with a 'Silver Spoon': The Origin of World Trade in 1571", *Journal of World History* 6:2 (Fall 1995), 201–221.
sources.perspective: Two economic historians arguing a thesis: world trade began in 1571 and China's demand for silver drove it. They write against a Europe-centred account. Their Pacific figures come from other scholars (Chuan, TePaske, Barrett), not from their own archive work.

position.focus: The world silver market from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century, with China as the main buyer.
position.note: On p. 204 they say Chuan built his Manila estimate from Blair and Robertson, the collection our SB01 to SB13 come from. Two of their page references do not match their own reference list (Chuan 1969, p. 79; "TePaske 1981").

sources.record: William S. Atwell, "International Bullion Flows and the Chinese Economy circa 1530–1650", *Past & Present* 95 (May 1982), 68–90.
sources.perspective: A historian of Ming China. He reads the silver trade for what it did to China's economy and to the dynasty. His Manila material comes from Schurz (1939), Ch'üan Han-sheng, Blair and Robertson, and Morga.

position.focus: Japanese and Spanish-American silver entering Ming China, and its effects there.
position.note: His 1573 cargo sentence (p. 73) comes through Schurz and matches the list in SB02; it is not an independent witness. His ratio table (p. 82) is from P'eng Hsin-wei.

sources.record: Richard von Glahn, *Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000–1700* (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1996), ch. 4, "Foreign Silver and China's 'Silver Century', 1550–1650", pp. 113–141.
sources.perspective: A historian of Chinese money, reading the silver trade from the Chinese side. His Manila figures come from Chaunu's customs series and TePaske; his Japan figures from Souza and Innes. He sets his own estimates below the ones most often quoted.

position.focus: How foreign silver reached Ming China from 1550 to 1650, by which routes and in what amounts.
position.note: The chapter's endnotes are not in our file. Its Manila series start in 1577 (ships) and 1586 (customs); it has no figure for 1573.

sources.record: Ubaldo Iaccarino, "The 'Galleon System' and Chinese Trade in Manila at the Turn of the 16th Century", *Ming Qing Yanjiu* 16 (2011), 95–128 (read pp. 95–96, 102–117, 121–122).
sources.perspective: A historian of the Chinese at Manila, working mainly from Spanish documents in Blair and Robertson and from Spanish and Chinese-language scholarship. His subject ends in the early 1590s; 1602 and 1603 appear only in passing.

position.focus: How the trade between Fujian and Manila became a fixed system between 1571 and the early 1590s.
position.note: He says America was China's main source of silver (p. 110); von Glahn says Japan was. His figures for the 1593 limits (p. 114) differ from Morga's.

sources.record: Arturo Giráldez and Dennis O. Flynn, "Arbitrage, China, and World Trade in the Early Modern Period", *Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient* 38:4 (1995), 429–448 (read p. 435).
sources.perspective: The authors of SB14 and SB15, the same year as SB14. They report the Mexico City council's figures and warn that nothing confirms them.

position.focus: The gap in silver's price between China and elsewhere, and the trade it drove.
position.note: Same authors as SB14 and SB15; not a separate witness.

sources.record: Pedro de Rojas to Felipe II, Manila, 1586. Blair & Robertson (eds.), *The Philippine Islands, 1493–1898*, vol. 6 (Cleveland, 1903), read p. 269. In English translation from the Spanish. [The letter's day, its full page range and its translator are to be taken from its first page and the volume's front matter, not yet opened.]
sources.perspective: A Spanish official at Manila complaining to the king about governors and soldiers who trade, and about the silver and gold the Chinese take away. He wants the trade restrained.

position.role: Licentiate; his office is not on the page read
position.interests: Restraining officials' trading and the outflow of silver

sources.record: Kris Lane, *Potosí: The Silver City That Changed the World* (Oakland: University of California Press, 2019), ch. 4, "An Improbable Global City", pp. 92–116 (read pp. 94, 96).
sources.perspective: A historian of Potosí, describing the town about 1600 from a description of 1603 and from merchants' inventories.

position.focus: Potosí as a town, about 1600: who lived there and what was sold.

sources.record: Pedro de Acuña, Governor of the Philippines, to the king, Manila, [18 December 1603, as Borao dates it (1998, p. 28)]. Blair & Robertson (eds.), *The Philippine Islands, 1493–1898*, vol. 12 (Cleveland, 1904), read p. 154. In English translation from the Spanish. [The letter's first page, its page range and its translator are to be taken from the volume, not yet opened.]
sources.perspective: The governor of the Philippines, writing to the king after the massacre of 1603 about the measures he had taken. He is giving his own account of them. He lays the trouble on 'restless and vagabond people who had nothing to lose' among the Chinese.

sources.record: José Eugenio Borao, "The Massacre of 1603: Chinese Perception of the Spanish on the Philippines", *Itinerario* 22:1 (1998), 22–40.
sources.perspective: A Spanish historian who sets the Spanish records of 1603 beside the Chinese ones and translates from both. He calls what was done a massacre and what began it an uprising, and says the reasons remain unclear.

position.focus: The killing of the Chinese of Manila in 1603, read from Spanish and Chinese records together.
position.note: Our only route to the Chinese records, which are official, anonymous and in Classical Chinese. His Spanish sources include Morga (our SR01) and letters printed in Blair and Robertson vol. 12.

sources.record: Katharine Bjork, "The Link That Kept the Philippines Spanish: Mexican Merchant Interests and the Manila Trade, 1571–1815", *Journal of World History* 9:1 (Spring 1998), 25–50 (read pp. 39–43).
sources.perspective: A historian arguing that merchants and officials in Mexico, not the crown, kept the Manila trade alive. Her dates for the bans on Peru come from Borah and Schurz, which we do not hold.

position.focus: Whose interests the Manila trade served, from the Mexican side.

sources.record: José Luis Gasch-Tomás, *The Atlantic World and the Manila Galleons* (Leiden: Brill, 2019), ch. 4, "Trans-Pacific Trade and the Political Economy of the Spanish Empire", pp. 91–128 (read pp. 115–124; the rest searched). [Author's first names and the book's subtitle to be confirmed on a title page.]
sources.perspective: A historian of the galleon trade working from the archives of Seville and Mexico City. He reads the limits on the trade as the outcome of bargaining among the merchants of Seville, Mexico City, Lima and Manila and the crown. On the bans on Peru he cites Borah and gives one year only.

position.focus: How rival merchant elites pressed the crown to limit, or to free, the trade across the Pacific.
position.note: He prints, in his own translation, a letter of the city council of Lima of 18 October 1599. His year for the first ban on Peru, 1582, differs by one from Bjork's and Iaccarino's.
